screens.title: Designing and Implementing Custom Policies
screens.narratorSegment: In enterprise blockchains, the default rules are a starting point, not the final word. In this lesson you will see how to design custom endorsement policies that precisely match who must approve a transaction. We’ll cover the three core logical operators—AND, OR, and NOutOf—how to set a signature-policy when approving and committing chaincode, and how Access Control Lists govern system chaincode actions. You’ll work through an example that deploys a chaincode requiring both Org1 and Org2 to endorse, and we’ll show how to test a failing invocation to confirm the policy. Why this matters: endorsement policies translate legal and business requirements into fabric-enforceable checks. A wrong policy can either block legitimate work or open a security hole. We’ll also summarize best practices so you can balance security with operational flexibility. By the end you’ll understand how to write policies, where to specify them, and how to validate them in a test network.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives guide focused practice. First, you will design endorsement policies using AND, OR, and NOutOf so each chaincode function reflects who must authorize it. For example, you should be able to write a policy that requires two out of three organizations to sign for high-value operations. Second, you will implement those policies during chaincode definition and commit. That means using the peer lifecycle approve and commit commands and specifying a signature-policy so Fabric enforces the rule at commit time. Third, you will learn how Access Control Lists work for system chaincode functions. ACLs in configtx. yaml map specific built-in functions to channel policies so system-level actions like lifecycle queries are restricted to the right roles. Fourth, you will apply best practices that balance security and usability: choose the appropriate operator, avoid hardcoding identities, test in development, and document the rationale. Each objective builds toward safe, maintainable policy design that aligns Fabric enforcement with your consortium’s real-world authorization needs.

screens.title: What is a Custom Endorsement Policy?
screens.narratorSegment: A custom endorsement policy is a Fabric-enforced rule that determines which peer identities or organizations must endorse a transaction before it can be considered valid. In plain terms, it encodes approval rules: who needs to sign for a transaction to proceed. For example, a policy might require both a buyer’s and a seller’s peer to endorse a transfer, or it might require any one of several auditors. This mapping from business roles to MSP identifiers is essential because policy logic is evaluated during the endorsement and validation phases of transaction processing. A common misconception is to treat policies as merely documentation; instead, they are executable checks enforced by Fabric’s orderer and validation steps. Another misconception is to hardcode individual certificate identities; don’t do that—use MSP IDs and roles so policies remain valid when certificates rotate. Concrete example: you can encode a requirement that Org1 and Org2 must both endorse a chaincode call by using a signature-policy string during chaincode approval. Takeaway: policies are the bridge from your real-world authorization model to Fabric’s enforcement, so design them carefully and test them thoroughly.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A custom endorsement policy is an executable rule that specifies which organizations or roles must endorse a transaction.

content.html:
Core Concept › Custom Endorsement Policy

Policy definition and role

A policy encodes which MSP roles or organizations must sign for a transaction to be valid. It is enforced by Fabric during endorsement and validation.

Why policies matter: translate legal approvals and consortium rules into code-enforced checks.
Misconception: policies are not documentation only; they are enforced at runtime.
Practical tip: reference MSP IDs and roles, not certificate serials.
Concrete example
Policy intent: require both Org1 and Org2 endorsements for transfers.
Visual mnemonic: two-person handshake — both must agree.
Key Takeaway

Policies are executable authorization rules. Design them to reflect roles, test them, and avoid hardcoding certificate identities.

screens.title: AND Operator
screens.narratorSegment: The AND operator requires endorsements from all listed identities or MSP roles for a transaction to be valid. This operator is best for actions that must have unanimous consent from named parties, such as cross-organizational transfers that must be approved by both sender and receiver organizations. A concrete example from the chapter: AND('Org1MSP. peer', 'Org2MSP. peer') requires a peer endorsement from Org1 and a peer endorsement from Org2. A common misconception is thinking AND is equivalent to majority; it is not. AND is strict: if any required organization cannot endorse because of downtime or a missing signature, the transaction will fail. Use AND when joint authorization is mandatory and downtime risk is acceptable. To mitigate availability problems, consider using NOutOf instead when you need resilience. Takeaway question: does this operation truly require all named organizations to approve, or could a quorum suffice? AND Operator means and demands endorsements from every named msp identity or role, suitable for strict joint approvals.. In practical terms, require every named organization to endorse a transaction. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: AND operator
keyIdea.text: AND demands endorsements from every named MSP identity or role, suitable for strict joint approvals.

content.html:
AND › Require all endorsers

AND — strict joint approval

Use AND when every named organization must sign. This is appropriate for high-value, cross-organization actions where all stakeholders must agree.

Example policy: AND('Org1MSP.peer', 'Org2MSP.peer')
When to use: joint approvals, escrow releases, cross-org asset transfers.
Common mistake: treating AND as majority; it requires every listed endorser.
Scenario
A payment requires both payer and receiver organizations to authorize a transfer. If either misses endorsement, Fabric will reject the transaction at validation.
Key Takeaway

AND is strict: choose it only when unanimity is required and acceptable operationally.

screens.title: OR Operator
screens.narratorSegment: The OR operator is the opposite of AND in practice: it permits a transaction to be valid if any one of the listed identities or organizations endorses it. This operator is useful when several parties can fulfill the same role and any single approver is acceptable. For example, OR('Org1MSP. peer', 'Org2MSP. peer') lets either Org1 or Org2 authorize the action. OR is often used to reduce friction where unanimous approval is unnecessary. A common misconception is assuming OR weakens security across the board; in fact, OR is appropriate when business rules allow delegated approval and when the role, not the specific org, matters. Consider where accountability and audit trails are still maintained, even if multiple organizations can approve. Takeaway: choose OR when flexibility is required and one responsible party suffices to enforce the rule. OR Operator means or allows any one listed organization or role to endorse, suitable when multiple parties can independently authorize an action.. In practical terms, allow any one of several organizations to endorse. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: OR operator
keyIdea.text: OR allows any one listed organization or role to endorse, suitable when multiple parties can independently authorize an action.

content.html:
OR › Any one endorser

OR — flexible approval

Use OR when several organizations can act in the same role and any single one is sufficient to approve. This reduces friction and speeds common operations.

Example policy: OR('Org1MSP.peer', 'Org2MSP.peer')
When to use: delegated approvals, alternative approvers, regional failover.
Common mistake: using OR where joint signature is required, reducing intended protections.
Scenario
A read-only approval may be satisfied by any member of a reviewer pool. OR lets a single reviewer sign without requiring full committee approval.
Key Takeaway

Choose OR when a single authorized party can reasonably represent the group’s consent.

screens.title: NOutOf Operator
screens.narratorSegment: NOutOf expresses quorum-style policies: NOutOf(2, 'Org1MSP. peer', 'Org2MSP. peer', 'Org3MSP. peer') requires any two of the listed organizations to endorse. This operator balances strictness and availability. It’s ideal for consortium operations where a majority, not unanimity, is required. A concrete example is a three-member consortium where at least two must approve asset transfers to prevent a single member from controlling actions. A common mistake is miscounting N or misplacing commas or parentheses when writing policy strings; test carefully. Compared to AND, NOutOf tolerates a temporarily unavailable organization while still enforcing multi-party approval. Compared to OR, it requires more than one signer, offering stronger assurance. Takeaway: use NOutOf when you need both multi-party endorsement and operational resilience against single-party downtime. NOutOf Operator means noutof specifies that any n of the listed organizations must endorse, offering quorum semantics for resilience and security.. In practical terms, quorum-based approval with resilience to unavailability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: NOutOf operator
keyIdea.text: NOutOf specifies that any N of the listed organizations must endorse, offering quorum semantics for resilience and security.

content.html:
NOutOf › Quorum approvals

NOutOf — quorum and resilience

NOutOf lets you require a specific count of endorsers out of a larger set, giving resilience when a participant is offline while still demanding multi-party approval.

Example: NOutOf(2, 'Org1MSP.peer', 'Org2MSP.peer', 'Org3MSP.peer')
When to use: consortium quorums, majority approvals, fault tolerance.
Common mistake: choosing N too high, blocking operations if multiple orgs are down.
Scenario
A consortium wants at least two approvals from three members. NOutOf ensures majority while allowing one member to be unavailable.
Key Takeaway

NOutOf gives you quorum semantics; pick N to balance security and availability.

screens.title: Setting the Signature Policy During Approval
screens.narratorSegment: Applying a custom policy happens during the chaincode definition approval and commit. The key step is passing a signature-policy string with the peer lifecycle approveformyorg command for each organization’s admin. This makes the policy part of the chaincode definition that will be committed to the channel. A concrete example from the chapter shows approving with a policy that requires Org1 and Org2: use the approve command and include a --signature-policy flag with AND('Org1MSP. peer','Org2MSP. peer'). A common mistake is forgetting to use identical policy strings when each org approves; the commit will fail if approvals do not match. Also, omitting the signature-policy flag will fall back to the default ImplicitMeta MAJORITY rule. After approvals, a commit command that repeats the --signature-policy ensures the committed definition carries the custom rule. Takeaway: treat the signature-policy as part of the chaincode definition and ensure all approvers use the same policy string to avoid commit-time mismatches. Setting the Signature Policy During Approval means specify --signature-policy during peer lifecycle chaincode approveformyorg so the definition records the required endorsements.. In practical terms, use peer lifecycle approveformyorg with a signature-policy to bind endorsements. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Apply policy at approval
keyIdea.text: Specify --signature-policy during peer lifecycle chaincode approveformyorg so the definition records the required endorsements.

content.html:
Process Flow › Approve with signature-policy

Approve with a custom signature-policy

Each organization’s admin runs the approval command and must include the identical signature-policy. This binds the endorsement rule to the chaincode definition.

# Example: approving a chaincode definition with a custom endorsement policy
peer lifecycle chaincode approveformyorg \
  -o localhost:7050 --ordererTLSHostnameOverride orderer.example.com --tls --cafile ${ORDERER_CA} \
  --channelID mychannel --name mychaincode --version 1.0 --package-id <PACKAGE_ID> \
  --sequence 1 --init-required \
  --signature-policy "AND ('Org1MSP.peer','Org2MSP.peer')"  # Custom policy here!
Test: ensure each org stores the same PACKAGE_ID and uses the same signature-policy string.
Pitfall: mismatched policies during approvals cause commit failures; keep strings identical.
Example walkthrough
After approval from each org, an authorized admin runs the commit command and includes the same --signature-policy so the channel records the custom endorsement rule.
Key Takeaway

The signature-policy is part of the chaincode definition. Approve and commit must agree on the same policy string.

screens.title: Default Policies and ImplicitMeta
screens.narratorSegment: If you omit a signature-policy when approving chaincode, Fabric uses the default channel-level policy behavior based on ImplicitMeta, typically a majority endorsement rule. The ImplicitMeta MAJORITY Endorsement policy requires a majority of organizations in the channel to endorse a transaction. This default can be useful for simple deployments but may not suit bespoke business rules. A common confusion is assuming default majority equals security best practice; in many consortiums, business logic calls for specific combinations of approvers, not just a majority. Another issue is that relying on defaults can hide misalignment between technical enforcement and legal agreements. Concrete example: if a chaincode performs highly sensitive financial transfers, the consortium might require explicit AND or NOutOf rules rather than implicit majority. Takeaway: explicitly set signature-policy when your business model needs specific endorsement combinations; rely on defaults only when majority semantics match your risk and process model. In practical terms, what happens when you don’t supply a signature-policy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: ImplicitMeta default
keyIdea.text: Omitting a signature-policy falls back to the channel’s ImplicitMeta MAJORITY endorsement, which may not match specific business rules.

content.html:
Definition › ImplicitMeta and defaults

ImplicitMeta MAJORITY

When --signature-policy is omitted, Fabric defers to the channel’s ImplicitMeta policy, commonly MAJORITY Endorsement. That means most members must endorse, not specific organizations.

Use case: small networks where majority consensus suffices.
Risk: implicit majority may not capture role-specific approvals required by business rules.
Advice: explicitly set a signature-policy when the business requires specific named approvers.
Scenario
If you deploy a payment chaincode and rely on default majority, you may allow approvals from a set of orgs that your policy writer didn’t intend. Explicit policies avoid this mismatch.
Key Takeaway

Defaults are convenient but can diverge from required approvals. Specify signature-policy when precision matters.

screens.title: ACLs and System Chaincode
screens.narratorSegment: Access Control Lists provide a different layer of control: they govern access to system chaincode functions rather than application chaincode endorsement. ACLs are configured in configtx. yaml under Application. ACLs and map a resource path to an existing channel policy. For instance, mapping _lifecycle/QueryChaincodeDefinition to /Channel/Application/Readers allows identities that satisfy the Readers policy to query chaincode definitions. If you want only channel admins to perform a query, map the resource to /Channel/Application/Admins instead. A common mistake is confusing ACLs with endorsement policies; ACLs control who can call system functions while endorsement policies control who must sign application transactions. Concrete example: to restrict lifecycle queries, add an ACL entry that points to the admin policy. Takeaway: use ACLs to secure built-in functions like lifecycle, qscc, and cscc, and make sure your mappings align with your operational access model. ACLs and System Chaincode means acls map system chaincode resources to channel policies in configtx.yaml, controlling who can invoke built-in functions.. In practical terms, map system functions to channel policies in configtx.yaml. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

ACLs secure system functions by mapping them to channel policies; set these deliberately to protect lifecycle and query operations.

screens.title: Deploying Chaincode with a Custom Policy
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on flow takes you through deploying chaincode with a custom endorsement policy requiring both Org1 and Org2. Step one is preparing the test network and channel so the peers exist and mychannel is created. Next you package the chaincode and install it on both organizations’ peers; record the PACKAGE_ID output for each install. content.html:
Hands-on Activity › Deploy with custom policy
Step-by-step
1. Start network
cd fabric-samples/test-network
./network.sh down
./network.sh up createChannel -c mychannel
2. Package chaincode
peer lifecycle chaincode package fabcar.tar.gz --path ../asset-transfer-basic/chaincode-go --lang golang --label fabcar_1.0
3. Install on peers
peer lifecycle chaincode install fabcar.tar.gz
# Record PACKAGE_ID from output
4. Approve with policy
peer lifecycle chaincode approveformyorg ... \
  --signature-policy "AND ('Org1MSP.peer','Org2MSP.peer')"
Commit and initialize
peer lifecycle chaincode commitchanneldefinition ... \
  --signature-policy "AND ('Org1MSP.peer','Org2MSP.peer')" \
  --peerAddresses localhost:7051 --peerAddresses localhost:9051
Test: invoke with both peers to succeed; invoke with only one peer to confirm it fails under the custom policy.
Key Takeaway

Follow the lifecycle steps carefully and verify the policy with both successful and failing invocations.

screens.title: Testing Policies and Common Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Testing a custom endorsement policy is straightforward and revealing. First, test a successful path: invoke the chaincode with the peerAddresses for every required endorser and confirm the transaction is accepted. Next, test a failing path: invoke with only a single endorser when the policy requires two and observe the endorsement failure message. This demonstrates the policy is enforced. Common mistakes to watch for include mismatched policy strings across approvals, different PACKAGE_ID values, or unintentionally using hardcoded certificate identities instead of MSP IDs. Another frequent error is confusing ACLs and endorsement policies; ACLs control system function access, not transaction endorsement. If commits fail, inspect the approval set and ensure each org approved the same policy string. For diagnosing, check peer and orderer logs and confirm the chaincode definition’s recorded policy. Takeaway: make test cases for both allowed and disallowed invocations, and log your test results so the consortium can reproduce and troubleshoot issues. content.html:
Testing › Common mistakes & checks

Test both success and failure

Create two tests: one that includes all required endorsers and one that omits some. Confirm Fabric accepts the first and rejects the second to validate the policy.

Success test: invoke with peerAddresses for all required endorsers.
Failure test: invoke with only one endorser when the policy requires two; expect endorsement failure.
Diagnostic: check approval records and peer logs if commit fails or behavior is unexpected.
Checklist
  • All orgs used the same --signature-policy string when approving.
  • PACKAGE_ID values match across installs.
  • Policies reference MSP IDs and roles, not certificates.
  • ACLs are configured separately for system functions.
Key Takeaway

Testing both allowed and denied paths is the most reliable way to confirm your policy behaves as intended.

screens.title: Design Principles and Documentation
screens.narratorSegment: Good policy design starts with understanding the underlying business process. Ask who must approve, why, and under what conditions. Use AND when unanimous consent is legally required, OR when any one authorized party suffices, and NOutOf for quorums that tolerate downtime. Avoid overly complex nested policies unless necessary; complexity raises operational risk. Don’t hardcode certificate identities—reference MSP IDs and roles so certificate rotation doesn’t break policies. Document each policy’s rationale: why you selected an operator, who is responsible, and how the policy aligns with governance. Always test in a development environment before committing to a production channel, and include both positive and negative test cases. Another best practice is to minimize the number of distinct policies to simplify audits and automation. Takeaway: well-documented, tested, and role-focused policies reduce confusion and operational failures across consortium members. Principles for maintainable policies

Understand business logic

Policies must reflect who legally or operationally must approve actions.

Balance security and usability

Avoid over-restrictive rules that block legitimate work; use NOutOf for resilience.

Clear, tested, and documented policies keep networks operational and auditable over time.

fullNarratorScript:
In enterprise blockchains, the default rules are a starting point, not the final word. In this lesson you will see how to design custom endorsement policies that precisely match who must approve a transaction. We’ll cover the three core logical operators—AND, OR, and NOutOf—how to set a signature-policy when approving and committing chaincode, and how Access Control Lists govern system chaincode actions. You’ll work through an example that deploys a chaincode requiring both Org1 and Org2 to endorse, and we’ll show how to test a failing invocation to confirm the policy. Why this matters: endorsement policies translate legal and business requirements into fabric-enforceable checks. A wrong policy can either block legitimate work or open a security hole. We’ll also summarize best practices so you can balance security with operational flexibility. By the end you’ll understand how to write policies, where to specify them, and how to validate them in a test network.

These objectives guide focused practice. First, you will design endorsement policies using AND, OR, and NOutOf so each chaincode function reflects who must authorize it. For example, you should be able to write a policy that requires two out of three organizations to sign for high-value operations. Second, you will implement those policies during chaincode definition and commit. That means using the peer lifecycle approve and commit commands and specifying a signature-policy so Fabric enforces the rule at commit time. Third, you will learn how Access Control Lists work for system chaincode functions. ACLs in configtx. yaml map specific built-in functions to channel policies so system-level actions like lifecycle queries are restricted to the right roles. Fourth, you will apply best practices that balance security and usability: choose the appropriate operator, avoid hardcoding identities, test in development, and document the rationale. Each objective builds toward safe, maintainable policy design that aligns Fabric enforcement with your consortium’s real-world authorization needs.

Now we connect objectives to practical actions. You will practice writing policies and applying them when you approve and commit a chaincode definition. For example, to require Org1 and Org2 to endorse, you will set a signature-policy during approval and confirm both organizations sign the definition. You will also create ACL mappings in configtx. yaml to limit who can call lifecycle or query functions, ensuring only readers or admins can perform those actions. Testing is essential: try invoking with only one peer and observe Fabric reject the transaction when the policy requires two endorsers. Finally, document each policy’s rationale so consortium members know why a rule exists. These applied objectives ensure you can both author the policy text and validate its enforcement on a test network, reducing the risk of deployment surprises in production.

A custom endorsement policy is a Fabric-enforced rule that determines which peer identities or organizations must endorse a transaction before it can be considered valid. In plain terms, it encodes approval rules: who needs to sign for a transaction to proceed. For example, a policy might require both a buyer’s and a seller’s peer to endorse a transfer, or it might require any one of several auditors. This mapping from business roles to MSP identifiers is essential because policy logic is evaluated during the endorsement and validation phases of transaction processing. A common misconception is to treat policies as merely documentation; instead, they are executable checks enforced by Fabric’s orderer and validation steps. Another misconception is to hardcode individual certificate identities; don’t do that—use MSP IDs and roles so policies remain valid when certificates rotate. Concrete example: you can encode a requirement that Org1 and Org2 must both endorse a chaincode call by using a signature-policy string during chaincode approval. Takeaway: policies are the bridge from your real-world authorization model to Fabric’s enforcement, so design them carefully and test them thoroughly.

The AND operator requires endorsements from all listed identities or MSP roles for a transaction to be valid. This operator is best for actions that must have unanimous consent from named parties, such as cross-organizational transfers that must be approved by both sender and receiver organizations. A concrete example from the chapter: AND('Org1MSP. peer', 'Org2MSP. peer') requires a peer endorsement from Org1 and a peer endorsement from Org2. A common misconception is thinking AND is equivalent to majority; it is not. AND is strict: if any required organization cannot endorse because of downtime or a missing signature, the transaction will fail. Use AND when joint authorization is mandatory and downtime risk is acceptable. To mitigate availability problems, consider using NOutOf instead when you need resilience. Takeaway question: does this operation truly require all named organizations to approve, or could a quorum suffice? AND Operator means and demands endorsements from every named msp identity or role, suitable for strict joint approvals.. In practical terms, require every named organization to endorse a transaction. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The OR operator is the opposite of AND in practice: it permits a transaction to be valid if any one of the listed identities or organizations endorses it. This operator is useful when several parties can fulfill the same role and any single approver is acceptable. For example, OR('Org1MSP. peer', 'Org2MSP. peer') lets either Org1 or Org2 authorize the action. OR is often used to reduce friction where unanimous approval is unnecessary. A common misconception is assuming OR weakens security across the board; in fact, OR is appropriate when business rules allow delegated approval and when the role, not the specific org, matters. Consider where accountability and audit trails are still maintained, even if multiple organizations can approve. Takeaway: choose OR when flexibility is required and one responsible party suffices to enforce the rule. OR Operator means or allows any one listed organization or role to endorse, suitable when multiple parties can independently authorize an action.. In practical terms, allow any one of several organizations to endorse. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

NOutOf expresses quorum-style policies: NOutOf(2, 'Org1MSP. peer', 'Org2MSP. peer', 'Org3MSP. peer') requires any two of the listed organizations to endorse. This operator balances strictness and availability. It’s ideal for consortium operations where a majority, not unanimity, is required. A concrete example is a three-member consortium where at least two must approve asset transfers to prevent a single member from controlling actions. A common mistake is miscounting N or misplacing commas or parentheses when writing policy strings; test carefully. Compared to AND, NOutOf tolerates a temporarily unavailable organization while still enforcing multi-party approval. Compared to OR, it requires more than one signer, offering stronger assurance. Takeaway: use NOutOf when you need both multi-party endorsement and operational resilience against single-party downtime. NOutOf Operator means noutof specifies that any n of the listed organizations must endorse, offering quorum semantics for resilience and security.. Good policy design starts with understanding the underlying business process. Ask who must approve, why, and under what conditions. Use AND when unanimous consent is legally required, OR when any one authorized party suffices, and NOutOf for quorums that tolerate downtime. Avoid overly complex nested policies unless necessary; complexity raises operational risk. Don’t hardcode certificate identities—reference MSP IDs and roles so certificate rotation doesn’t break policies. A few final condensed concepts to close the chapter. NOutOf provides quorum semantics where N of a set must endorse, ideal for fault tolerance. The --signature-policy flag is the mechanism you use during peer lifecycle approve and commit to attach a custom policy to a chaincode definition. Access Control Lists in configtx. yaml map system chaincode functions to existing channel policies, controlling who can invoke lifecycle queries, configuration reads, or other built-in operations. Keep these distinctions clear: endorsement policies govern transaction validity, ACLs govern access to system functions, and signature-policy binds a chosen endorsement policy to a chaincode definition.
